slides.title: How big is the universe?
bullets: The universe contains more than 200 billion galaxies.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, contains around 200–400 billion stars.
Our Sun is just one of those stars.
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old — it began with the Big Bang.

slides.title: From the Big Bang to our solar system
bullets: The Big Bang: everything began from a tiny, incredibly hot point.
Over billions of years, matter clumped together to form stars and galaxies.
Our Milky Way galaxy formed about 13.5 billion years ago.
Our solar system formed about 4.5 billion years ago inside the Milky Way.

slides.title: Meet the solar system
bullets: My Very Energetic Mother Just Served Us Noodles — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
The Sun is a star — it produces its own heat and light. The planets do not.
In 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet — there are now officially 8 planets.
Beyond our solar system there are billions of other star systems in the Milky Way.

slides.title: The order of the planets
bullets: The four closest planets to the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky.
The four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are much larger and made mainly of gas.
Jupiter is the largest planet — more than 11 times wider than Earth.
Saturn's famous rings are made of ice and rock.

slides.title: What does the data tell us?
bullets: Planet diameters range from 4,879 km (Mercury) to 142,984 km (Jupiter).
Average distances from the Sun range from 57.9 million km (Mercury) to 4,495 million km (Neptune).
Pattern: the further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year (orbital period).
Pattern: the four inner planets are much smaller than the four outer planets.

slides.title: Day, night and the seasons
bullets: Day and night: Earth rotates once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.
Sunrise is always in the east; sunset is always in the west.
Seasons: Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5°. As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere tilts towards or away.
When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun → summer. Tilts away → winter.

slides.title: What do you think about the Moon?
bullets: The Moon is always in the sky — it can be seen during the day as well as at night.
The Moon does not produce its own light — it reflects sunlight.
The Moon orbits Earth once every 27–29 days, causing the phases.
The phases are not caused by Earth's shadow — they are caused by which part of the lit Moon we can see.

slides.title: Moon phases and lunar eclipses
bullets: New Moon → Crescent → Half (First Quarter) → Gibbous → Full Moon → Gibbous → Half (Third Quarter) → Crescent → New Moon.
A lunar eclipse happens when Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon.
Lunar eclipses only happen at full Moon.
The Moon is always present — we just can't always see it clearly.

slides.title: Rocky planets vs gas giants
bullets: Rocky (terrestrial) planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — small, solid surface, closer to the Sun.
Gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — huge, made mainly of gas, further from the Sun.
Temperature pattern: the closer a planet is to the Sun, the higher its average temperature.
Exception: Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being further away — because of its thick atmosphere.

slides.title: Relative clauses in action
bullets: A relative clause adds information about a noun: 'Saturn, which has rings made of ice and rock, is the sixth planet from the Sun.'
Use 'which' for things, 'who' for people, 'where' for places.
The relative clause is usually separated from the main clause by commas.
Without the relative clause the sentence still makes sense: 'Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun.'

slides.title: Three ways to use parenthesis
bullets: Brackets: 'Mars (the fourth planet from the Sun) is roughly half the size of Earth.'
Dashes: 'Neptune — the furthest planet from the Sun — takes 165 Earth years to complete one orbit.'
Commas: 'Venus, the hottest planet in our solar system, has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide.'
All three add extra information — the main sentence must still make sense if you remove the parenthesis.

slides.title: Our three-paragraph structure
bullets: Paragraph 1 — Introduction: the solar system, Earth's place within it, why your chosen planet is interesting.
Paragraph 2 — The chosen planet: key facts, conditions, size, distance from Sun, moons, rings, surface.
Paragraph 3 — Comparison: how does your chosen planet compare to Earth? Size, temperature, day length, conditions.
Each paragraph begins with a topic sentence that tells the reader what is coming.
